clinicalPearls: SPG44 is an autosomal recessive complicated HSP caused by biallelic mutations in GJC2 (also called GJA12), which encodes the oligodendrocyte gap-junction protein connexin-47.
It lies at the mild end of the connexin-47 disease spectrum, being allelic with Pelizaeus-Merzbacher-like disease type 1 (PMLD1).
Compared with classic PMLD1, SPG44 has later onset (childhood to adulthood) and a slower, milder course, often without the early infantile pendular nystagmus and hypotonia.
Core features are spastic paraparesis, dysarthria, mild cognitive impairment and cerebellar signs including ataxia and nystagmus.
Upper-limb involvement and a subclinical or mild peripheral neuropathy may be present.
MRI shows a diffuse hypomyelinating leukoencephalopathy, sometimes with a thin corpus callosum.
Connexin-47 couples with astrocytic connexin-43 to form the panglial gap-junction network that is essential for myelin homeostasis.
A milder, hypomorphic GJC2 genotype tends to produce SPG44 rather than the severe infantile PMLD1 phenotype.
reference.pathophysiology: SPG44 results from biallelic mutations in GJC2 on chromosome 1q42, the gene encoding connexin-47 (Cx47), a gap-junction protein expressed predominantly by oligodendrocytes. Connexin-47 pairs with astrocytic connexin-43 to build the panglial syncytium through which ions, water and metabolites are buffered across the myelin unit; loss of functional Cx47 channels disrupts this coupling and impairs the formation and maintenance of central myelin, producing a hypomyelinating leukodystrophy. Milder, often hypomorphic, alleles preserve enough residual channel function to yield the comparatively indolent SPG44 phenotype, whereas more severe loss-of-function alleles cause infantile-onset Pelizaeus-Merzbacher-like disease type 1, placing the two disorders on a single allelic continuum.
additionalDifferentials: Pelizaeus-Merzbacher-like disease type 1 (PMLD1) — the severe allelic counterpart
Pelizaeus-Merzbacher disease and SPG2 (PLP1) — X-linked hypomyelination
TUBB4A-related hypomyelination with atrophy of the basal ganglia and cerebellum (H-ABC)
Metachromatic leukodystrophy and other lysosomal leukodystrophies
Other complicated HSPs with white-matter change (e.g. SPG11, SPG15)
additionalInvestigations: MRI brain to identify the diffuse hypomyelination pattern and assess the corpus callosum
GJC2 (GJA12) sequencing, or a hypomyelinating leukodystrophy / HSP gene panel
Nerve conduction studies to detect any peripheral neuropathy
Visual and brainstem auditory evoked potentials
Arylsulfatase A activity and very-long-chain fatty acids to exclude other leukodystrophies
Ophthalmological review for nystagmus and visual function
redFlags: Severe infantile onset with pendular nystagmus and marked hypotonia, pointing to the PMLD1 end of the spectrum
reference.prognosis: SPG44 is generally milder and more slowly progressive than PMLD1; many affected individuals remain ambulant into adult life, although spasticity, ataxia and dysarthria accumulate over time.
pitfalls: Mislabelling the child as having cerebral palsy because early motor delay and spasticity overlap
Failing to recognise the hypomyelination pattern on MRI, which can be mistaken for simple delayed myelination
Not appreciating the continuum with PMLD1, so that a GJC2 result is misinterpreted in isolation
Overlooking mild cerebellar or neuropathic signs that indicate a complicated rather than pure HSP
references: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
GeneReviews — hereditary spastic paraplegia and connexin-47-related disorders
Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics
management: Symptomatic antispasticity therapy with baclofen or tizanidine, and botulinum toxin for focal spasticity
Physiotherapy, stretching and orthoses to maintain mobility, with balance and gait training for the cerebellar ataxia and provision of walking aids
Educational and neuropsychological support for the mild cognitive impairment
Serial MRI monitoring of the hypomyelinating leukoencephalopathy and neurological progression
Genetic counselling for autosomal recessive inheritance and carrier testing of relatives
Multidisciplinary neurology, rehabilitation, speech therapy and neuropsychology input
